questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Grouping checks by what they prove
questions.learningObjective: Group validation checks by the property they establish
questions.stem: Explain how you would group the checks applied to a movement authority into categories by the property each one establishes.

answer.exemplar: A useful way to sort checks is by the claim each one can support. Checks that establish provenance answer the question of where a value came from: a valid signature against the issuing office's key shows the office issued it, and a chain to a trusted authority shows the office itself is recognised. Checks that establish currency answer whether the value still counts: an expiry time, a not-before time, a maximum age, and a count of uses left. Checks that establish fitness answer whether this particular holder may use this particular value for this particular action: a role in the token, a scope on it, a permission list on the account, a destination on the movement. When the categories are kept apart, it is easy to notice that a token can be genuine and current and still not be fit for the job, and that a permission list can be perfect while the provenance of the value is unchecked.

questions.explanation: Grouping by property separates what each check proves: a signature shows the origin, an expiry shows currency, and a permission check shows fitness for the movement. Gaps then show as empty categories.
questions.hint: Sort the checks by the claim each supports.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Traffic that leaves outside the tunnel
questions.learningObjective: Explain why off-tunnel traffic escapes the link's protection
questions.stem: Explain why traffic that a dispatcher sends to an external supplier's server is not covered by the protection on the control link, even when it is requested by the control panel.

answer.exemplar: The control link protects a specific path: the sequence of hops between the dispatcher's terminal and the control room, and it secures everything carried along that path. When the control panel asks a supplier's server for a help page, the request does not travel along that path to the control room. It leaves the terminal, crosses the public network and the supplier's own links, and arrives at a server the control room has no authority over and no protected route to. From that moment the exchange depends on whatever the supplier has arranged, and the request and reply are outside the control link's protection. This matters whenever the panel mixes in content from elsewhere, because it is easy to assume that anything the panel shows the dispatcher is as protected as the panel itself, when in fact only the parts that stay inside the tunnel are.

questions.explanation: The link protects the path between dispatcher and control room. A request to a supplier's server leaves that path for infrastructure the control room does not control, so protection stops at the boundary.
questions.hint: Ask where the request travels after the terminal.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Three settings on one cookie
questions.learningObjective: Explain the independent risks closed by cookie settings
questions.stem: Explain how the three settings on a session cookie each reduce a different risk, and why none of them can be replaced by another single setting.

answer.exemplar: The three settings on a session cookie are often described as hygiene, but each one closes a different door. The setting that hides the cookie from scripts closes the path where injected script on the dispatcher's own page reads the value and posts it elsewhere. The setting that restricts the cookie to protected links closes the path where the value is carried in the clear over a shared network and read from the packet. The setting that restricts it to same-site requests closes the path where a page on another site makes the browser attach the cookie to a request to the control room, so the attacker obtains the value without ever touching it. None of the three can stand in for another. Hiding a cookie from scripts does nothing about a network observer, refusing unprotected links does nothing about a cross-site request, and refusing cross-site requests does nothing about script access. They are cheap, independent and each answers a question the others leave open.

questions.explanation: One stops scripts reading the cookie, one stops it crossing unprotected links, one stops it riding on cross-site requests. They cover three paths to misuse, so each is needed.
questions.hint: Ask what misuse each setting closes off.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a second check leaves open
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a second check may not reduce a stolen-value risk
questions.stem: Explain why adding a second check to a session value does not necessarily reduce the risk of a stolen cookie being used.

answer.exemplar: The value of a second check depends entirely on what it inspects. A stolen cookie is a bit-for-bit copy of a value that was legitimate when it was taken, so anything the server can learn from the value itself, its signature, its claims and its expiry, will read exactly as it did for the real dispatcher. Re-checking those properties, or adding a second signature over the same material, adds effort without changing the outcome. The checks that do change the outcome are the ones that ask something the copied value cannot answer: does the client still come from the address that signed in, does the holder still know the second factor, does the server see a fresh proof of presence rather than a replayed value. That is the difference between making a value harder to forge and making a copy harder to use, and only the second kind of check closes the gap left by an interception.

questions.explanation: A stolen cookie copies a valid value, so a second check on the value's properties passes for it too. What helps is checking what the copy lacks, such as the holder's address or fresh identity.
questions.hint: Ask whether the copy can answer the new check.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The life of a session value
questions.learningObjective: Describe the full lifecycle of a session value
questions.stem: Describe the life of a session value from the moment it is issued to the moment it is finally refused.

answer.exemplar: The life of a session value runs through four stages, and each stage closes a different way for an old copy to be used. It starts when the server issues a value that it records against the dispatcher's authenticated state; at this point the value means nothing to anyone who guesses it, which is why it must be unpredictable. It then travels on every request, which is convenient for the client and invisible to the dispatcher, and this is the stage at which the value can be copied. It is then rotated, so that the server accepts the replacement and refuses the original, limiting how long one captured copy remains useful. Finally it expires, and after that the server refuses it regardless of what the client presents. Rotation and expiry do different jobs, and rotation exists to make a captured value age faster than a stolen password would.

questions.explanation: The server issues it, the client presents it on each request, it is rotated so older copies stop working, and it expires on a schedule. It is rejected when the server meets an unknown or expired value.
questions.hint: Ask what ends each stage of the value's life.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Three settings on one cookie
questions.learningObjective: Explain how cookie settings reduce the chance of a copied value
questions.stem: Explain how the three settings on a session cookie reduce the chance that a stolen copy of the value can be used against the control room.

answer.exemplar: A stolen cookie is a problem of obtaining a copy as much as of using one, and each of the three settings removes a different route to that copy. Hiding the cookie from scripts removes the route where the dispatcher's own machine is running a page that was tampered with, because injected code cannot reach a cookie it cannot read. Restricting the cookie to protected links removes the route where somebody sitting on the same network captures the value as it travels. Restricting it to same-site requests removes the route where an attacker hosts a page that silently causes the browser to send the value to the control room, so the attacker never needs to read the cookie at all. None of these makes the value impossible to take; a machine that is already fully controlled can still read what the browser holds. They simply remove the ordinary, low-effort ways of obtaining a copy.

questions.explanation: Each setting blocks a different way of copying the value: script access, network capture, or a cross-site return. None substitutes for another, so the value is harder to take, though never impossible.
questions.hint: Ask how the copy could have been obtained.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Three settings on one cookie
questions.learningObjective: Explain which party enforces cookie settings
questions.stem: Explain who actually enforces the three settings on a session cookie, and what follows from that.

answer.exemplar: It is worth being precise about where a cookie setting does its work. The control room's server writes the settings into the response header, and that is all it does. The instruction is then carried out by the browser: only the browser knows whether a page on another origin is trying to set the cookie, only the browser knows which links it is about to follow, and only the browser is in a position to decide that a particular request originated elsewhere. If the browser honours those instructions, the value is kept away from scripts, kept off plain links and kept off cross-site requests. If the browser is old, is configured to ignore some of these, or is replaced by something that does not read them at all, the setting is simply a line of text that nobody acts on. This is the reason cookie settings are described as defences in depth rather than as guarantees, and the reason the server's own code should never assume that the browser has complied.

questions.explanation: The server only states the settings; the browser reads and obeys them. Protection depends on browser compliance, so an outdated browser weakens the result with no change on the server.
questions.hint: Ask which party actually obeys the settings.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a session value stands in for
questions.learningObjective: Explain the value of rotating a session value
questions.stem: Explain why a session value is safer to rotate than to leave long-lived, even when the transport carrying it is protected.

answer.exemplar: Protecting the transport and shortening the life of the value are two different defences, and the second is what limits the damage of a copy. The transport protects the value while it travels between the dispatcher and the control room. It says nothing about the value once it is in the browser's memory, where any script that can read it may take a copy, nor about the copy that may already have been taken months ago and been sitting on someone's disk. That copy is a perfectly valid credential and the server has no way to tell it from the live one. Rotation is what eventually neutralises it: the server stops accepting the old value and issues a replacement, so a copy made at any point in the past stops working after the next rotation rather than remaining usable until some distant expiry. The protected transport limits where a copy can be taken; rotation limits how long a taken copy is worth.

questions.explanation: A protected transport keeps the value unreadable in transit, but it still sits in the browser, in the server's records and in any earlier copy. Rotation shortens how long a copy stays useful.
questions.hint: Ask how long a captured copy remains useful.

answer.exemplar: Two checks are often called two when they are really one, because each answers half of a single question and neither half is useful on its own. A movement authority can be perfectly genuine and perfectly unusable at the same time, and it can be perfectly current and entirely forged. The signature speaks to the first problem and the expiry to the second, and together they say one thing: this is a document the issuing office produced and this document may still be acted on. questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Three settings on one cookie
questions.learningObjective: Match cookie settings to the routes they close
questions.stem: A dispatcher opens the panel, which loads a script from a partner's domain, and the panel also sends a session cookie on every request. First, state whether the cookie settings protect against that script; second, state what they do protect against.

options.text: They protect against the script, and they also stop the value being read off the network
options.misconception: credits the settings with script protection

options.text: They do not stop the script directly, but they stop the value riding along on that partner's requests
They protect against the network, and they also stop the script reading the value
options.misconception: credits the settings with script protection

options.text: They protect against neither, because the cookie settings only apply to the control room's own domain
options.misconception: denies the settings any effect at all

questions.explanation: The settings keep the value on the control room's origin and off plain links, so a partner script cannot obtain it by riding along and an observer cannot read it in flight. They do not protect the machine.
questions.hint: Ask where the cookie is allowed to travel.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Grouping checks by what they prove
questions.learningObjective: Separate the properties covered by three checks
questions.stem: A control room wants to know what its three checks on a movement authority each establish. Which statement gives the correct set?

options.text: They establish origin, currency and fitness for this movement, and together they also identify who is presenting
options.misconception: adds holder identity to the three checks

options.text: They establish origin, currency and fitness, but each one can be satisfied without the other two
options.misconception: treats the three properties as independent guarantees

options.text: They establish the holder's identity, the current time and the movement's priority
options.misconception: substitutes different properties for the real ones

options.text: They establish origin, currency and fitness for this movement, while the holder's identity comes from the sign-in

questions.explanation: The three checks cover origin, currency and fitness for this movement, and none of them names the holder. The tempting answers add identity to the set or swap in unrelated properties.
questions.hint: Ask what each check looks at.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: The life of a session value
questions.learningObjective: Compare the expiry of an original and a replacement value
questions.stem: A dispatcher's session value was issued at 06:00 with a 12-hour life. The dispatcher signed off at 17:00, and a replacement value was issued at 17:00 with a 1-hour life. Which statement describes the record correctly?

options.text: The replacement runs to 18:00 and the original ran to 18:00 as well, since twelve hours from 06:00 is 18:00
The replacement runs to 18:00 and the original expired at 17:00 when the dispatcher signed off
options.misconception: assumes sign-off expires the value immediately

options.text: The replacement runs to 05:00 the next day, since a one-hour life starts at sign-in
options.misconception: moves the start of the new value's life

options.text: The replacement runs to 17:00, since it was issued at the moment the old one ended
options.misconception: reads a one-hour life as zero validity

questions.explanation: Twelve hours from 06:00 is 18:00, so the original and the one-hour replacement end together. The tempting answers expire the value at sign-off or read a one-hour life as no time.
questions.hint: Add each life to the moment it started.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Two checks that are really one
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two checks form one assurance
questions.stem: Explain why a signature check and an expiry check on the same value are often described as two halves of one assurance rather than as two separate protections.

answer.exemplar: Neither half is sufficient alone: a signature on an expired value is useless, and an unexpired value with a bad signature could be anyone's. Together they answer whether the office issued it and it may still be acted on. Describing them as two halves of one assurance rather than as two protections is a statement about what each half is for. A protection is something that stands between the value and a harm, and each of these checks is a condition on the value rather than a barrier. Calling them two separate protections invites the belief that defeating one leaves the other standing, and that belief is exactly what fails, because an attacker who presents an unexpired value with a broken signature has defeated the pair rather than half of it.

questions.explanation: Neither half is sufficient alone: a signature on an expired value is useless, and an unexpired value with a bad signature could be anyone's. Together they answer whether it may be used.
questions.hint: Ask what each half fails to establish alone.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: What a session value stands in for
questions.learningObjective: Count session values issued over a working week
questions.stem: A dispatcher signs in 4 times on each of 5 working days, and each sign-in produces one session value. How many session values are issued across that week?
questions.explanation: Four sign-ins on each of 5 days gives 20 sign-ins, and each produces one value, so 20 values are issued across the week. The tempting answer of 9 adds the figures and the answer of 5 counts days.
questions.hint: Multiply sign-ins per day by days.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Traffic that leaves outside the tunnel
questions.learningObjective: Read which requests a protected link covered

stimulus.body: Inspection of the dispatch terminal's network traffic for one hour: every request to the control room was carried inside the protected line, while eleven requests to a contractor's map server were carried outside it on plain routes, showing full destination headers and payload sizes.

questions.stem: What does this report show about the panel's traffic?

options.text: The protected line was misconfigured, because control room traffic travelled on plain routes
options.misconception: misreads which traffic was unprotected

options.text: All the panel's traffic was protected, because the terminal's own connection is protected
options.misconception: assumes one protected link covers every request

options.text: The contractor's map requests were protected, because they were the only ones with visible headers
options.misconception: treats visible headers as evidence of protection

options.text: Control room traffic was covered by the protected line, and the eleven external requests were not

questions.explanation: Control room requests travelled on the protected line and the eleven contractor requests travelled outside it in the clear, so coverage depends on destination. The tempting answers blame the line or read headers as protection.
questions.hint: Ask which requests left the protected path.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Traffic that leaves outside the tunnel
questions.learningObjective: State how many requests leave a protected link and what it means
questions.stem: A dispatch panel makes 100 requests an hour, and 8 of them go to an external map service while the rest go to the control room over the protected line. First, state how many requests leave the protected line; second, state what that means for the panel.

options.text: Eight requests leave the protected line, so those responses are not covered by the control link's protection
Ninety-two requests leave the protected line, because the panel is not on the protected line
options.misconception: reverses which group is covered

options.text: Eight requests leave the protected line, so the panel as a whole cannot be trusted
options.misconception: generalises from a leak to the whole panel

options.text: Eight requests leave the protected line, so the external service must also be trusted
options.misconception: assumes off-link traffic implies trust

questions.explanation: Only the 8 external requests leave the protected line, so those responses are not covered while the other 92 are. The tempting answers reverse the groups or generalise from one leak.
questions.hint: Ask which group is outside the link.
